title: GraphQL Federation: A Field Guide
summary: A dense study-notes handbook on GraphQL federation — how subgraphs, entity keys, reference resolvers, and gateway query planning combine one supergraph out of many services — with a hard-nosed comparison against schema stitching and the operational traps teams hit in production.

chapters.title: Why Federation Exists
points: Monolithic GraphQL server: one schema, one team owning it, becomes a merge-conflict bottleneck as org grows
Federation = compose one client-facing schema (the supergraph) from many independently deployed services (subgraphs)
Core promise: clients see one endpoint and one type system; teams own and deploy slices independently
Contrast with REST-per-service + BFF: BFF hand-writes stitching logic, federation derives it from schema metadata
Terminology: subgraph = service + its schema; supergraph = composed schema + routing metadata; gateway/router = runtime executing it
Separation of concerns: subgraph schema is the API contract, supergraph SDL is a build artifact, never hand-written
Apollo Federation v1 (2019) → v2 (2022) added shared ownership directives (@shareable, @override, @interfaceObject)
Alternatives in the same space: Apollo Federation, GraphQL Mesh, Cosmo, Hive Gateway, Netflix DGS (federation-compatible)
Key design constraint: subgraphs must never call each other's GraphQL APIs directly — the gateway orchestrates
Federation is a spec + set of directives, not a single vendor product; multiple routers implement the same contract
Anti-goal: federation is not a general API gateway, not a caching layer, not a service mesh
When NOT to federate: one team, one deploy, <2 services — the composition overhead outweighs the ownership win
Cost of entry: composition pipeline, schema registry, CI checks, a router in the hot path of every request

chapters.title: Subgraphs: Anatomy of a Federated Service
points: A subgraph is a normal GraphQL server plus federation directives and two extra root fields
`_service { sdl }`: returns the subgraph's raw SDL including directives, used by composition
`_entities(representations: [_Any!]!): [_Entity]!`: the gateway's entry point for fetching entities by key
`_Entity` is a generated union of every type in the subgraph that has an `@key`
`_Any` is a scalar: an untyped JSON blob carrying `__typename` plus key fields
Subgraph libraries (`@apollo/subgraph`, graphql-java federation, strawberry, gqlgen) generate these automatically
Each subgraph owns the *fields* it defines, not the whole type — `User.email` in accounts, `User.orders` in orders
Example: `type Product @key(fields: "id") { id: ID!, name: String!, price: Int! }` in the products subgraph
Example: `type Product @key(fields: "id") { id: ID!, reviews: [Review!]! }` in the reviews subgraph — same type, new fields
Root `Query`/`Mutation` types are implicitly shared; every subgraph may contribute root fields
Federation v2: types are contributable by default; v1 required `extend type` on non-owning subgraphs
`@link(url: "https://specs.apollo.dev/federation/v2.3", import: ["@key", "@shareable"])` at the top opts a schema into v2
Subgraphs should be independently runnable and testable — you should be able to query one directly in dev
Naming discipline: two subgraphs defining `User` differently (different key, different meaning) is a composition error, not a merge

chapters.title: Entities and @key
points: An entity = a type identifiable across subgraph boundaries by a stable key; the unit of federation
`@key(fields: "id")` declares that field set uniquely identifies an instance of the type
Key field sets use a selection-set mini-language: `"id"`, `"sku upc"` (compound), `"organization { id } email"` (nested)
A type may declare multiple `@key`s: `@key(fields: "id") @key(fields: "sku")` — the gateway picks one the source subgraph can supply
Every subgraph that contributes fields to an entity must declare a `@key` matching one the owner exposes
`@key(fields: "id", resolvable: false)` — this subgraph references the entity but cannot resolve it; used for pure references
Key fields must be present and non-null in every subgraph declaring them, or resolution fails at runtime
Value types (no `@key`) are duplicated by value across subgraphs and must be structurally identical to compose
Entity vs value type decision: does it have an identity that outlives the request? Then it's an entity
Bad key smell: keys derived from mutable data (email, slug) break caching and cross-subgraph joins on update
Compound key gotcha: `@key(fields: "a b")` means *both* fields together identify the entity — all must travel in the representation
Nested keys require the referenced type to be reachable and its fields selectable in the referencing subgraph
`@key` on an interface (v2.3+, `@interfaceObject`) lets a subgraph add fields to all implementations at once
Design rule: the key is a permanent public contract — changing it is a breaking change for every subgraph that references the type

chapters.title: Reference Resolvers
points: A reference resolver answers: "given this key, hydrate the rest of this entity from my data"
JS signature: `__resolveReference(reference, context, info)` where `reference` is `{ __typename, ...keyFields }`
Example: `Product: { __resolveReference: ({ id }, { dataSources }) => dataSources.products.byId(id) }`
The gateway batches keys into one `_entities(representations: [...])` call per subgraph per plan step
Representations arrive as an *array* — a naive per-key resolver produces N+1 database queries
Fix: DataLoader (or equivalent batch loader) keyed on the entity key, scoped to the request context
Return `null` from a reference resolver for a dangling reference; the field resolves to `null`, not an error
Returning a partial object is fine — remaining fields resolve through normal field resolvers
The reference resolver is not called if every requested field is already satisfiable from the key
Ordering: `_entities` MUST return results positionally matching the input representations array
Type resolution for interfaces/unions inside `_entities` uses `__typename` from the representation
Auth inside reference resolvers: they run out of the original query's context path, so re-check authorization per entity
Cost model: each hop in a plan is one network round trip plus one batch fetch — deep entity chains multiply latency
Testing tactic: call `_entities` directly with hand-written representations to unit-test a subgraph's join surface

chapters.title: Field-Level Directives
points: `@external`: this field is defined in another subgraph; declared here only so local directives can reference it
`@requires(fields: "...")`: this resolver needs extra fields from the owning subgraph before it can run
`@requires` example: `shippingCost: Int! @requires(fields: "weight dimensions { l w h }")` with `weight` marked `@external`
`@provides(fields: "...")`: this subgraph can return a neighbor's fields inline, letting the planner skip a hop
`@provides` is an optimization only — it must be truthful or clients see stale/wrong data
`@shareable`: multiple subgraphs may resolve this field; without it, duplicate non-key fields fail composition
`@override(from: "subgraphName")`: migrate ownership of a field from one subgraph to another with no downtime
Progressive `@override(from: "x", label: "percent(25)")` routes a fraction of traffic to the new owner
`@inaccessible`: field exists in the supergraph for composition but is hidden from the public API schema
`@tag(name: "...")`: metadata for contracts/variants — build a public schema that excludes `@tag(name: "internal")`
`@extends`: legacy v1 marker equivalent to `extend type`, still accepted for interop
`@composeDirective`: lifts a custom directive from a subgraph into the supergraph so the router can see it
`@interfaceObject`: treat an interface as a concrete type in one subgraph and add fields to all implementers
Directive gotcha: `@requires` fields are fetched in an extra planner step — every `@requires` is a potential extra round trip

chapters.title: Composition: Building the Supergraph
points: Composition takes N subgraph SDLs and produces one supergraph SDL, or a list of composition errors
The supergraph SDL carries `@join__` directives encoding which subgraph owns which field
`rover supergraph compose --config supergraph.yaml` for local builds; managed federation composes in the registry
Composition is deterministic and offline — no service needs to be running to compose
Common error: `FIELD_TYPE_MISMATCH` — same field, different types across subgraphs
Common error: `INVALID_FIELD_SHARING` — two subgraphs resolve the same non-key field without `@shareable`
Common error: `KEY_FIELDS_MISSING_EXTERNAL` / unresolvable key — subgraph declares a key it cannot satisfy
Common error: `SATISFIABILITY_ERROR` — a valid query exists that the planner has no path to execute
Satisfiability is the deep check: composition proves every possible query shape is reachable, not just that types merge
Enum merging: input-position enums intersect, output-position enums union — a mismatched enum can break composition
Schema registry (Apollo GraphOS, Hive, Cosmo) stores versions, runs checks against real traffic, and publishes the supergraph
CI schema checks compare a proposed subgraph against the registry and against operation traffic to flag breaking changes
Publish flow: subgraph CI → `rover subgraph publish` → registry composes → router hot-reloads supergraph, no restart
Rollback discipline: deploy the subgraph code before publishing the schema on additions; reverse the order on removals

chapters.title: The Gateway and Query Planning
points: The router parses the client operation, builds a query plan against the supergraph, then executes it
A query plan is a tree of nodes: `Fetch` (call a subgraph), `Sequence` (ordered), `Parallel` (concurrent), `Flatten` (path into the response)
Planning is a search over possible subgraph paths, scored by number of fetches and depth — it is the expensive part
Query plan caching keys on the normalized operation; cold plans for large schemas can take tens of milliseconds
Persisted queries / safelisting let the router pre-plan and skip parsing+planning per request
Step 1 fetch hits an *entry point* subgraph — one that owns a root field in the operation
Later steps send `_entities` calls with representations extracted from earlier responses via the `Flatten` path
Sibling branches with no data dependency plan as `Parallel`; `@requires` forces `Sequence`
Response is stitched back into the client's requested shape; `__typename` is injected automatically to route entities
Apollo Router (Rust) replaced the Node `@apollo/gateway` for throughput; same planning semantics, far lower overhead
Inspect plans in dev: `?dry-run` / the `query-planner` trace in Apollo Explorer, or `ApolloServerPluginInlineTrace`
Cross-cutting concerns live in the router: auth header propagation, rate limiting, APQ, response caching, telemetry
Router does NOT retry subgraph errors by default — a partial failure surfaces as `errors` plus `null` in `data`
Deep fetch chains are the #1 federation latency bug — read the plan before blaming the database

chapters.title: Federation vs Schema Stitching
points: Schema stitching: the gateway holds hand-written type merging config and delegates with `delegateToSchema`
Federation: the *subgraphs* declare their join contract via directives; the gateway derives routing automatically
Ownership of join logic — stitching: centralized in the gateway; federation: distributed to the services
Adding a cross-service field — stitching: edit the gateway repo; federation: edit only the subgraph, republish
Deploy coupling — stitching: gateway redeploy on schema change; federation: router hot-reloads the supergraph
Conflict handling — stitching: rename/transform via schema transforms; federation: composition rejects the build
Correctness — stitching: mistakes surface at runtime; federation: satisfiability is proven at composition time
Non-GraphQL sources — stitching (and Mesh) wraps REST/gRPC/OpenAPI easily; federation needs a subgraph shim
Legacy/third-party schemas you cannot modify — stitching wins outright; you cannot add `@key` to someone else's server
Ecosystem — stitching lives in `@graphql-tools`; federation has Apollo, Cosmo, Hive, Mesh (which speaks both)
Cost — stitching has no composition pipeline or registry; federation requires that build infrastructure
Choose stitching for: few schemas, no subgraph-code control, heterogeneous non-GraphQL backends
Choose federation for: many teams, real service ownership, and a need for compile-time guarantees
GraphQL Mesh can present stitched sources *as* a federated subgraph — the two are combinable, not exclusive

chapters.title: Trade-offs, Failure Modes, and Operations
points: Latency math: a client query touching 3 subgraphs in a chain costs 3 serial round trips, not 1
N+1 across the boundary: 100 products × 1 reviews fetch each — only avoided by `_entities` batching + DataLoader
Partial failure semantics: one subgraph 500s, the router returns valid `data` with `null` holes plus an `errors` entry
Nullability is the blast radius — a non-null field failing propagates the null up to the nearest nullable ancestor
Timeouts and circuit breaking belong in the router; a slow subgraph otherwise pins gateway connections
Authorization: the router forwards headers, but each subgraph must independently authorize — never trust the gateway alone
Do not put the user's identity in a subgraph-only context and assume other subgraphs have it; propagate explicitly
Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) is non-optional — a single client query becomes N spans across N services
Query cost/depth limiting must run at the router, before planning, or a malicious query fans out across services
Caching layers: APQ (request size), query plan cache (planning cost), entity cache (subgraph fetch cost) — different problems
Anti-pattern: a "god subgraph" owning most entities — you rebuilt the monolith plus a network hop
Anti-pattern: chatty entity chaining, A→B→C→A, when a single subgraph could own the join
Anti-pattern: federating by technical layer (db-subgraph, cache-subgraph) instead of by business domain
Testing pyramid: subgraph unit tests → `_entities` contract tests → composition checks in CI → supergraph smoke tests

chapters.title: Putting It Together: A Worked Supergraph
points: Scenario: three subgraphs — accounts (`User`), products (`Product`), reviews (`Review`) — one storefront query
accounts: `type User @key(fields: "id") { id: ID!, name: String! }` plus `Query.me: User`
products: `type Product @key(fields: "upc") { upc: String!, name: String!, price: Int! }` plus `Query.topProducts: [Product]`
reviews: `type Review { body: String!, author: User, product: Product }` with `User`/`Product` re-declared by key
reviews adds `type User @key(fields: "id") { id: ID! @external, reviews: [Review] }` — the cross-service join
Client query: `{ me { name reviews { body product { name price } } } }` — spans all three subgraphs
Plan: Fetch(accounts, `me{id name}`) → Flatten(me) → Fetch(reviews, `_entities` for User) → Flatten(reviews.product) → Fetch(products, `_entities` for Product)
Three round trips, but only three — every review's product resolves in one batched `_entities` call
Add `Review.product @provides(fields: "name")` and the products fetch disappears when only `name` is asked for
Migrating `Product.price` from products to a new pricing subgraph: add it there with `@override(from: "products")`, ship, then delete the old field
Local dev loop: `rover dev` runs router + subgraphs and recomposes on file change
Recap: entities are the nouns, `@key` is their identity, reference resolvers are the join implementation, the plan is the query engine
Recap: federation buys team autonomy and compile-time correctness; it costs round trips and a build pipeline
Final rule of thumb: model subgraphs on domain boundaries you would defend in a design review, not on your current service topology
